title: Bill calls for forensic survey of land at former reform school where Black youth are buried
summary: Del. Jeffrie Long Jr. says his bill to investigate the deaths of Black youth who died in state care and were buried in forgotten graves dating back to the 19th century is not symboic but is "an act of accountability, an act of dignity, an act of restoration."
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 19, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 19, 2026

Del. Jeffrie Long Jr. (D-Calvert and Prince George’s) testified Thursday about a visit he and several members of the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland made last year to a dilapidated wooded area in Prince George’s County where as many as 300 Black youth are believed to be buried.

Long said on that warm September day he led a prayer while standing amid the gravesites — some dating to the 19th century — and cinder blocks that mark where other youth are buried. The land was once home to the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children, and borders the pristine Cheltenham Veterans Cemetery in Long’s district.

Long was testifying before the House Government, Labor and Elections Committee (GLE) as sponsor of House Bill 552, which calls for a forensic anthropology and archaeological investigation of the site to discover if there may be more unmarked graves.

According to a Capital News Service review of death certificates, newspaper articles and grand jury reports on the deaths of 142 of the youth at the House of Reformation many died of tuberculosis and pneumonia.

“The state assumed responsibility for them in life, and we carry responsibility for them in death,” Long told the committee. “I want to be very clear, though, that this is more than just symbolism because naming the unnamed is not symbolic. It is an act of accountability, an act of dignity, an act of restoration.”

Long said his bill would be amended to conform to the Senate version sponsored by Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery).

The Senate bill, which will be heard Wednesday before the Judicial Proceedings Committee, calls for the creation of a commission to “research the history, operations, and resident deaths” at the former House of Reformation property.

More than a dozen people would serve on the commission, including the director of the Maryland Historical Trust, state archivist, secretary of the Department of Juvenile Services, secretary of General Services and the Prince George’s County executive, or their designees. The attorney general would serve as the commission chair.

During Thursday’s bill hearing, Acting Juvenile Services Secretary Betsy Fox Tolentino arrived to testify in support of the legislation. The department was recently awarded a $200,000 grant to pay for a ground-penetrating radar survey and restoration of the cemetery grounds.

“We support the core purpose of ensuring a full and public accounting of the children who died while confined at the House of Reformation for Colored Children, and acknowledging a painful chapter in Maryland’s history,” Fox Tolentino said. “Proper memorialization, education and respectful treatment of the burial sites are essential steps towards accountability and community healing.”

According to the House bill’s fiscal note, another $250,000 is budgeted toward restoration efforts starting in fiscal 2027 and in the next two fiscal years.

“While this analysis assumes $250,000 annually, the Department of Legislative Services (DLS) notes that the exact expenditures required to complete the investigation required by the bill are unknown and depend in part on challenges that may arise during the course of the investigation,” the note states.

Long said that amount could decrease because the bill would require the attorney general’s office to provide staff for the commission.

The bill requires the commission to submit a report by Dec. 31, 2027, to document the progress of the investigation with preliminary recommendations to the governor and General Assembly. A final report is due exactly two years later to include all individuals identified and the circumstances of their deaths, historical analysis of institutional policies and practices and “recommendations for acknowledgement, memorial, reburial, reparative measures and policy reforms.”

Del. Melissa Wells (D-Baltimore City), who chairs the GLE committee, suggested Long get a letter of support from the Legislative Black Caucus, which made the reformation effort one of its priorities.
